w: Founded in 1379 by Bishop William of Wykeham alongside his own feeder school at Winchester, New College was among the first in Oxford built to actually tutor undergraduates. Its lane passes the city's mock Bridge of Sighs, and its choir has cut past a hundred albums, twice winning a Gramophone Award.

w: Univ stakes a claim to being Oxford's oldest college, founded by William of Durham in 1249. Its alumni run from Stephen Hawking and C.S. Lewis to Bill Clinton and two British prime ministers, and it counts Christian Cole, the university's first Black graduate, among its own.

w: Somerville opened in 1879 as one of Oxford's first two women's colleges, deliberately non-denominational at a university steeped in Anglican gatekeeping. It stayed women-only until 1994 and in 1964 was among the first to stop locking students in at night. Alumnae include Margaret Thatcher and Dorothy L. Sayers.

w: Lady Margaret Hall opened in 1879 alongside Somerville as one of Oxford's first two women's colleges, on a bend of the River Cherwell. It took its name from Lady Margaret Beaufort, who also founded two Cambridge colleges, and in 2016 became the only Oxbridge college running a Foundation Year for disadvantaged students.

w: Walter de Merton, chancellor to two kings, drew up statutes here in the 1260s for something new: a self-governing academic community with its own endowments. Mob Quad, finished by 1378, is claimed as Oxford's oldest quadrangle, and Merton's library, dating to 1373, is the oldest working university library on Earth.

w: Founded in 1314 by two Devon brothers, a bishop and a knight, to educate clergy, Exeter has sat on Turl Street since 1315 as Oxford's fourth-oldest college. Its rooms later shaped very different storytellers: J.R.R. Tolkien here, decades before Philip Pullman and Alan Bennett passed through the same gate.

w: Sir Thomas White founded St John's in 1555 to train Roman Catholic clergy for the Counter-Reformation, a project the Reformation soon overtook. What endured was the land: as ground landlord of Victorian Oxford suburbia, the college became Oxford's wealthiest, assets past seven hundred million pounds.

w: A widow's will founded Wadham in 1610: Dorothy Wadham carried out her husband's bequest and raised one of Oxford's finest Jacobean quadrangles. Decades later, under warden John Wilkins, scientists including Christopher Wren and Robert Boyle met here regularly - gatherings that grew into the Royal Society.

w: Christ Church Cathedral is the only English cathedral that also serves as a college chapel, a dual role nobody planned. The first church here burned in the St Brice's Day massacre of 1002; Cardinal Wolsey suppressed the priory in 1524 meaning to flatten it, but his fall from grace in 1529 saved the building.

It has since become the single image everyone reaches for to signify Oxford, though it's now just a closed reading room.

w: Sir Thomas Pope founded Trinity in 1555 on ground once held by Durham College, home to Benedictine monks before the dissolution swept them out. Despite a small student body of around 400, Trinity has produced three British prime ministers, third-most behind only Christ Church and Balliol.

w: Adam de Brome founded Oriel in 1324 under Edward II's patronage, Oxford's oldest royal foundation - the reigning monarch is still its official visitor. Its site absorbed four medieval halls, including Tackley's Inn, the oldest standing medieval hall in the city. Oriel was the last men's college to admit women, in 1985.

w: Jesus College was chartered by Elizabeth I in 1571, pushed into being by Hugh Price, a Welsh churchman from Brecon. Its oldest quad still stands from the 1500s, tucked between Turl Street and Cornmarket. Alumni include Harold Wilson, twice prime minister, and T.E. Lawrence - Lawrence of Arabia.

William Butterfield's neo-Gothic design was controversial, and broke with tradition by lining rooms along corridors instead of staircases - so scouts could keep watch.

Restored and extended with new wings across the 16th and 17th centuries, it still functions as a working reading room today.

w: St George's Tower here predates the rest of Oxford Castle, a Saxon watchtower before the Normans raised a motte-and-bailey around it and fought over it through the Anarchy. Its military use faded by the 1300s, and it settled into life as a county prison - one that kept operating as HM Prison Oxford until 1996.
